screens.title: Analog Input: Reading Sensors with analogRead()
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll make the Arduino a simple bridge between the continuous physical world and your digital code. The Uno's analog input uses a 10‑bit converter to sample a voltage and produce a number between zero and 1023. That raw number is not yet a physical measurement until you convert it into volts or a sensor-specific unit like degrees Celsius. You will learn the formula to turn ADC values into voltage, how common sensors like potentiometers and temperature sensors produce readable voltages, and how to scale and calibrate those readings so they match real world units. We'll practice with a potentiometer feeding analog pin A0, display live values to the Serial Monitor, and use the map function to re-scale ranges. By the end, you will know how to check your reference values, interpret ADC resolution, and avoid common pitfalls that reverse or mis-scale your data. Think of the ADC as a ruler with 1024 marks across 5 volts; learning to read and scale that ruler makes sensors useful and reliable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Analog Input

Analog Input: Reading Sensors with analogRead()

Turn continuous voltages into usable numbers, convert those numbers into volts or sensor units, and calibrate for accuracy.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Animated explainer, code panels, and hands-on steps
In this lesson you will: read analog values, convert to volts, calibrate sensors, and map ranges for practical use.
Orientation

The Arduino does not measure analog in human terms by default. It measures voltage steps. We will use the built-in ADC reading, a simple conversion formula, and sensor conversion factors so your program understands physical quantities like volts or degrees.

Ruler Analogy
10-bit ruler: 0–1023 across 5 volts
Quick formula
float voltage = (analogRead(A0) / 1023.0) * 5.0;
Use this conversion to translate raw readings into voltage before applying sensor-specific scaling.
Coming up
  • Potentiometer circuit and live Serial Monitor example
  • Temperature sensor conversion with LM35 example
  • Calibration and using the map function safely
Key Topics
ADC resolution and range
Analog sensors and voltage dividers
Calibration and mapping to units
Hands-on preview
Connect a potentiometer to A0, print raw and converted voltage to the Serial Monitor, then use the knob to control an LED blink rate. That simple loop ties sensor reading to output control.

First, you will learn the ADC concept: a 10‑bit converter mapping 0 to 1023 across the reference voltage. Second, you will practice reading values from analog pins A0 through A5 and use the conversion formula to get volts. Third, you will apply sensor conversion factors, for example using the LM35's ten millivolts per degree Celsius, and walk through a worked example. Fourth, you will perform a simple calibration using bright and dark readings or known temperature points and safely use the map function to rescale values. Each objective pairs a practical coding step with an explanation of why it matters for accuracy. These competencies let you turn sensor voltages into meaningful measurements for control, logging, and user feedback.

screens.title: What the ADC actually measures
screens.narratorSegment: The analog-to-digital converter is a sampling device that assigns an integer to a measured voltage. On the Uno the ADC has ten bits of resolution, which means the input range is divided into 1,024 steps numbered from zero to 1,023. A helpful mental model is a ruler scaled from 0 to 1023 that spans the reference voltage—by default five volts. When the ADC samples a pin it reports the closest mark on that ruler. For example, a mid-scale reading around 512 means the input sits roughly halfway across the reference voltage. This discrete stepping is why two different voltages can sometimes report the same reading if they land within the same step. That limitation is called quantization. It matters because if your signal swings in a very small range, the ADC may not resolve those small changes. To improve effective resolution you change the input range or amplify the sensor signal, but on the Uno the default approach is to understand the 0–1023 granularity and design sensors and scaling around it. Consider this question as you read values: am I measuring small enough changes to be visible on a 10‑bit scale?

keyIdea.title: ADC definition
keyIdea.text: The ADC reports discrete integer steps from 0 to 1023 representing the measured voltage across the reference range; this creates quantization that affects measurement precision.

content.html:
Core Concept

10‑bit resolution and quantization

The ADC divides the reference voltage into 1024 discrete steps. Each sample returns the index of the closest step, not the exact analog voltage.

Ruler analogy
Imagine a ruler with marks from 0 to 1023 stretched across 5 volts. The reading finds the nearest mark to your input voltage.
Quick bullets
  • 0 equals 0 volts, 1023 equals the reference voltage (default 5V).
  • Resolution step size = reference / 1023; on 5V that is about 4.887 mV per step.
  • Quantization means small voltage changes smaller than one step may be invisible.
Key Takeaway

Understand the ADC as a discrete ruler. If your sensor output moves less than a single ADC step, you must amplify or change the measurement strategy.

Concrete example

With a 5V reference each ADC step is about 4.887 millivolts. A signal that swings 2 mV will not change the ADC reading; a 10 mV swing will usually change it by about two counts. Keep step size in mind when selecting sensors.

Common misconception

Do not assume analogRead directly gives a voltage. It gives a count that must be converted. Treat the raw number as an index on the ADC ruler, not as the physical unit itself.

screens.title: Using analogRead() and reading pins
screens.narratorSegment: Reading an analog sensor in Arduino code is a simple two-step loop: call analogRead on a pin and interpret the returned integer. The function returns values from zero to 1023 and accepts pin names like A0 through A5. A typical validation practice is to print the raw reading and the converted voltage to the Serial Monitor so you can inspect both at once. For example, read the raw count, compute voltage using the conversion formula, and print both with a short delay. This shows if wiring or sensor behavior matches expectations before you use the value in control logic. When you observe the Serial output, try turning a potentiometer or changing light and notice how the count responds. If the reading stays steady at 0 or 1023, check wiring and reference voltage. Also remember that analogRead returns an integer, so if you need sub-step precision you must compute using floating point after the read. The habit of serial validation reduces debugging time and ensures your program uses accurate, understood inputs. Using analogRead() and reading pins means call analogread(a0) to get a 0–1023 integer. always validate by printing raw counts and converted voltage to the serial monitor before using values in control code.. In practical terms, how to capture raw adc counts from a0–a5 and validate readings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: analogRead usage
keyIdea.text: Call analogRead(A0) to get a 0–1023 integer. Always validate by printing raw counts and converted voltage to the Serial Monitor before using values in control code.

content.html:
Process Flow

Call, convert, validate

Read raw counts with analogRead, convert to voltage using the ADC formula, and print both to confirm behavior.

// In setup
Serial.begin(9600);
// In loop
int raw = analogRead(A0);
float voltage = (raw / 1023.0) * 5.0;
Serial.print(raw); Serial.print(" \t"); Serial.println(voltage);
Validation steps
  • Print raw and voltage to verify wiring and expected range.
  • Turn the potentiometer: the raw value should sweep from near 0 to near 1023.
  • If stuck at extremes, check power, ground, and the pins used.
Concrete scenario

Wire a potentiometer between 5V and ground, middle pin to A0. Upload the code, open Serial Monitor, and turn the knob. You should see numbers climb smoothly from low counts to high counts and corresponding voltages from near 0 to near 5 volts.

Common misconception

Don't assume a stable analogRead means a correct scale. Always inspect converted voltage too; a raw value alone doesn't reveal reference or wiring errors.

Key Takeaway

Use analogRead then convert and validate with Serial printing. This simple loop saves time and clarifies sensor behavior.

screens.title: Converting ADC counts to voltage
screens.narratorSegment: Converting ADC counts to a voltage is a straightforward calculation but critical to understand. The formula uses the raw integer from analogRead, divides by the top ADC index 1023.0 to produce a fraction of the reference, and multiplies by the reference voltage. With the default five volt reference the formula is float voltage = (analogRead(A0) / 1023.0) * 5.0. Use a floating point divisor so you keep fractional precision. A concrete example: if analogRead returns 143, divide 143 by 1023 giving about 0.1398, multiply by 5 to get about 0.699 volts. If you then have a sensor that produces 10 millivolts per degree, that voltage corresponds to roughly 69.9 degrees. Always pay attention to units: the formula produces volts, not millivolts or degrees. If you need millivolts multiply by 1000. If you need different reference voltage, replace 5.0 with your reference value. Finally, beware integer division: writing 1023 instead of 1023.0 can truncate results in some languages, so ensure floating arithmetic is used in the calculation. Converting ADC counts to voltage means use voltage = (raw / 1023.0) * vref to convert adc counts into volts; always use floating point math and correct units.. In practical terms, use the conversion formula and check units. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Voltage conversion
keyIdea.text: Use voltage = (raw / 1023.0) * Vref to convert ADC counts into volts; always use floating point math and correct units.

content.html:
Definition

ADC to voltage formula

Apply the fraction of full scale and multiply by the reference voltage. Use floating math to keep precision.

Formula
voltage = (raw / 1023.0) * Vref
With Vref = 5.0: voltage = (raw / 1023.0) * 5.0
Notes
  • Result is in volts. Multiply by 1000 for millivolts.
  • Replace 5.0 with your actual reference if different.
  • Use 1023.0 to avoid integer division truncation.
Worked example

Given raw = 143 and Vref = 5.0: 143 / 1023.0 = 0.1398; multiply by 5 gives about 0.699 volts. If a sensor outputs 10 mV per degree, 0.699 V equals approximately 69.9 degrees.

Common misconception

Do not interpret the raw ADC number as a unit of temperature or percent. Convert to the sensor's physical unit using the sensor's scale after converting to volts.

Key Takeaway

Always convert raw counts to volts first, then apply sensor-specific conversion factors. Check your math with a concrete example to build confidence.

screens.title: Potentiometer and voltage divider circuits
screens.narratorSegment: A potentiometer is one of the simplest analog sensors because it directly produces a voltage between two rails when you move the knob. It is a three‑pin device: one outer pin to 5V, the other outer pin to ground, and the middle pin gives a variable voltage that moves between 0 and 5 volts as you rotate the shaft. That movable terminal is the output the Arduino reads on an analog pin. Wiring it this way forms a voltage divider: a portion of the supply voltage appears at the center pin proportional to the knob position. This makes the potentiometer ideal for adjustable controls like volume, brightness, or speed. When wiring, ensure the middle pin goes to the analog input, and the ground and 5V rails are common with the Arduino. Also be mindful of mechanical limits: if the knob goes to an extreme and the ADC reports values near 0 or 1023, that is expected; if the values never reach extremes, check that the outer pins truly connect to 5V and ground. Finally, treat potentiometers as low-impedance sources for best readings and avoid long high-resistance wiring which can introduce noise.

keyIdea.title: Potentiometer principle
keyIdea.text: A potentiometer wired between 5V and ground presents a variable voltage on its middle pin; the Arduino reads that voltage directly with analogRead.

content.html:
Definition

Potentiometer as a voltage divider

Wire the outer pins to 5V and ground, and the middle pin to an analog input. The middle pin yields a variable voltage proportional to knob position.

5V
Wiper (A0)
GND
Checklist
  • Outer pins to 5V and ground, middle to A0.
  • Share common ground with the Arduino board.
  • Expect values near 0 and 1023 at the ends of travel.
Concrete example

Use a 10k potentiometer: middle pin to A0, one outer to 5V, other outer to ground. Turn the knob and observe the Serial Monitor values sweep from near 0 to near 1023. Use the same reading to control an LED blink rate or brightness in code.

Common mistake

Wiring the wiper to power or ground instead of the analog pin will not produce a usable reading. Always confirm the wiper middle pin is connected to the analog input.

Key Takeaway

A potentiometer gives a reliable, easy-to-read voltage when wired as a divider. Validate with serial prints and use it to control outputs directly.

screens.title: Other analog sensors and conversion
screens.narratorSegment: Many sensors change resistance or output a small voltage in response to physical conditions. Light-dependent resistors and flex sensors typically change resistance and are read using a voltage divider. Temperature sensors like the LM35 or TMP36 produce a voltage that is proportional to temperature; the LM35 produces ten millivolts per degree Celsius as a simple example. The conversion pattern is consistent: read the ADC, convert counts to volts, then apply the sensor's scale factor to get the physical unit. For the LM35 example, a measured voltage of 0.699 V corresponds to about 69.9 degrees Celsius when using the ten millivolts per degree factor. Always check the sensor datasheet for the exact relationship and units because each sensor may have offsets or different scaling. When using resistive sensors like an LDR, select the fixed resistor in the divider so the voltage range matches the ADC steps you need. This lets your readings cover the useful range and improves sensitivity where you need it most. Other analog sensors and conversion means apply a two-step conversion: adc counts to volts, then volts to sensor units using the sensor's scale factor or datasheet formula.. In practical terms, ldrs, lm35/tmp36, flex sensors — convert voltages with sensor data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sensor conversions
keyIdea.text: Apply a two-step conversion: ADC counts to volts, then volts to sensor units using the sensor's scale factor or datasheet formula.

content.html:
Comparison

Sensor types and conversion steps

Voltage-output sensor (LM35)
Read ADC → convert to volts → apply 10 mV/°C to compute temperature.
Resistive sensor (LDR, flex)
Use a voltage divider with a fixed resistor → read ADC → convert to volts → map to desired scale.
Worked conversion

Example: raw = 143 → voltage ≈ 0.699 V. For LM35 with 10 mV/°C, temperature ≈ 0.699 / 0.01 = 69.9 °C. Use the sensor's datasheet to confirm offsets and linearity.

Common misconception

Resistive sensors need proper divider design. Swapping the fixed resistor can shift the voltage range and sensitivity; choose values so the ADC sees the sensor's useful range.

Key Takeaway

Always consult the sensor datasheet for scaling and offsets, and design your divider so the sensor output maps well onto the ADC's 0–1023 range.

screens.title: Calibration and using map()
screens.narratorSegment: Calibration makes sensor readings meaningful and comparable. A common two-point method for a light sensor is to record the ADC value in bright light and in complete darkness, then use those two measurements as your brightValue and darkValue. The map function rescales a raw ADC count from that measured range to a chosen target range such as 0 to 100 percent. For example, capture darkValue and brightValue, then write int percent = map(raw, darkValue, brightValue, 0, 100). Always ensure darkValue is less than brightValue. If you feed map reversed values the result will be inverted or unpredictable. Map performs integer scaling; if you need smooth fractional values, convert to float and compute scaling manually. Calibration also helps compensate for sensor variance and ambient conditions. For repeatable results, document your reference measurements, test at multiple points, and consider repeating calibration if environmental conditions change. Calibration converts relative readings into interpretable, actionable numbers. Calibration and using map() means use two reference readings and the map function to rescale raw adc values; ensure your reference ordering is correct and choose floating math when you need fractional precision.. In practical terms, collect reference points and rescale readings safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Calibration principle
keyIdea.text: Use two reference readings and the map function to rescale raw ADC values; ensure your reference ordering is correct and choose floating math when you need fractional precision.

content.html:
Process Flow

Two-point calibration and mapping

Capture a low and high reference, then rescale raw readings into a useful range with map or manual scaling.

Step 1
Measure darkValue and brightValue from the sensor.
Step 2
Use map(raw, darkValue, brightValue, 0, 100) to compute percent.
Step 3
Verify ordering: darkValue must be less than brightValue to avoid inversion.
Common pitfall

Reversed reference values produce reversed output. Check your captured references before using map.

Concrete example

If darkValue = 120 and brightValue = 900, mapping a raw value of 510 yields roughly middle percent. Use float math for smoother scaling when needed and record calibration values for reproducibility.

Key Takeaway

Calibration turns raw counts into meaningful ranges. Capture references carefully and double-check ordering before mapping.

keyIdea.title: End-to-end example
keyIdea.text: Use a potentiometer to drive Serial output and control an LED; map raw ADC values to a delay or PWM range to see analog input drive behavior.

content.html:
Hands-on activity

Potentiometer → Serial → LED

Read the pot, convert to volts, print values, then map the raw reading to control an LED blink delay or brightness.

// setup
Serial.begin(9600); pinMode(9, OUTPUT);
// loop
int raw = analogRead(A0); float v = (raw / 1023.0) * 5.0;
Serial.print(raw); Serial.print(" \t"); Serial.println(v);
int delayMs = map(raw, 0, 1023, 50, 1000); digitalWrite(9, HIGH); delay(delayMs); digitalWrite(9, LOW); delay(delayMs);
Misconception to avoid

Using map with wrong reference endpoints can produce non-intuitive control ranges. Always confirm the mapping endpoints by observing Serial output first.

Scenario and tweaks

If you want smooth brightness, map raw to 0–255 and write to a PWM pin with analogWrite. If the pot seems insensitive around the center, consider a non-linear mapping or different fixed resistor values for greater sensitivity where you need it.

Key Takeaway

This single project demonstrates reading, conversion, mapping, and output control—core skills for sensor-driven projects.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When readings don't match expectations there are a few common causes to check in order. First, confirm wiring and shared ground. A missing common ground or miswired potentiometer often explains stuck values like 0 or 1023. Second, validate the reference voltage assumption: the conversion formula assumes the default five volts; if your circuit uses a different reference the computed volts will be off. Third, inspect your code for integer division or lack of floating math causing truncated results. Fourth, consider sensor wiring: resistive sensors must form a proper voltage divider and the fixed resistor chosen affects sensitivity. Fifth, remember the ADC has finite resolution; very small changes under a single step will not appear in readings. Finally, check for reversed mapping when using map(): ensure your low and high reference values are ordered correctly. The best debugging sequence is to print the raw ADC value, the converted voltage, then the final scaled unit. That reveals where the mismatch appears so you can fix wiring, math, or calibration. content.html:
Comparison

Where things typically fail

  • Wiring: misconnected pot pins or missing common ground.
  • Reference mismatch: using the wrong Vref in conversion.
  • Integer math: accidental truncation instead of float math.
  • Divider selection: fixed resistor choice moves sensitivity.
  • Quantization: small signals below one ADC step won't show.
Debug routine
  1. Print raw ADC reading to Serial.
  2. Print converted voltage using the formula.
  3. Compare the computed unit (e.g., °C) to expected values and check sensor datasheet.
  4. Adjust wiring or calibration as needed and repeat.
Key Takeaway

A short print-and-compare routine isolates whether a problem is wiring, math, or calibration—start there before changing hardware or code significantly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll make the Arduino a simple bridge between the continuous physical world and your digital code. The Uno's analog input uses a 10‑bit converter to sample a voltage and produce a number between zero and 1023. That raw number is not yet a physical measurement until you convert it into volts or a sensor-specific unit like degrees Celsius. You will learn the formula to turn ADC values into voltage, how common sensors like potentiometers and temperature sensors produce readable voltages, and how to scale and calibrate those readings so they match real world units. We'll practice with a potentiometer feeding analog pin A0, display live values to the Serial Monitor, and use the map function to re-scale ranges. By the end, you will know how to check your reference values, interpret ADC resolution, and avoid common pitfalls that reverse or mis-scale your data. Think of the ADC as a ruler with 1024 marks across 5 volts; learning to read and scale that ruler makes sensors useful and reliable.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain how the Uno's analog-to-digital converter works, read analog sensor values with analogRead(), convert those raw numbers into volts or physical units, and calibrate sensors using known reference points. First, you will learn the ADC concept: a 10‑bit converter mapping 0 to 1023 across the reference voltage. Second, you will practice reading values from analog pins A0 through A5 and use the conversion formula to get volts. Third, you will apply sensor conversion factors, for example using the LM35's ten millivolts per degree Celsius, and walk through a worked example. Fourth, you will perform a simple calibration using bright and dark readings or known temperature points and safely use the map function to rescale values. Each objective pairs a practical coding step with an explanation of why it matters for accuracy. These competencies let you turn sensor voltages into meaningful measurements for control, logging, and user feedback.

These objectives map to short exercises you can try right away. You will run code that prints raw ADC counts and the converted voltage to the Serial Monitor, so you learn to validate readings before using them. You will wire a potentiometer as a voltage divider and use the knob to control an LED blink rate, which shows how analog readings can become control signals. You will convert a sample ADC reading into temperature using a sensor's conversion factor, such as ten millivolts per degree Celsius for an LM35, and check your arithmetic against a known reference. Finally, you will perform a two-point calibration for a light sensor by capturing dark and bright ADC values and using the map function to produce a 0 to 100 percent range. Each practice ties an abstract number back to a physical quantity, improving both accuracy and interpretability.

The analog-to-digital converter is a sampling device that assigns an integer to a measured voltage. On the Uno the ADC has ten bits of resolution, which means the input range is divided into 1,024 steps numbered from zero to 1,023. A helpful mental model is a ruler scaled from 0 to 1023 that spans the reference voltage—by default five volts. When the ADC samples a pin it reports the closest mark on that ruler. For example, a mid-scale reading around 512 means the input sits roughly halfway across the reference voltage. This discrete stepping is why two different voltages can sometimes report the same reading if they land within the same step. That limitation is called quantization. It matters because if your signal swings in a very small range, the ADC may not resolve those small changes. To improve effective resolution you change the input range or amplify the sensor signal, but on the Uno the default approach is to understand the 0–1023 granularity and design sensors and scaling around it. Consider this question as you read values: am I measuring small enough changes to be visible on a 10‑bit scale?

Reading an analog sensor in Arduino code is a simple two-step loop: call analogRead on a pin and interpret the returned integer. The function returns values from zero to 1023 and accepts pin names like A0 through A5. A typical validation practice is to print the raw reading and the converted voltage to the Serial Monitor so you can inspect both at once. For example, read the raw count, compute voltage using the conversion formula, and print both with a short delay. This shows if wiring or sensor behavior matches expectations before you use the value in control logic. When you observe the Serial output, try turning a potentiometer or changing light and notice how the count responds. If the reading stays steady at 0 or 1023, check wiring and reference voltage. Also remember that analogRead returns an integer, so if you need sub-step precision you must compute using floating point after the read. The habit of serial validation reduces debugging time and ensures your program uses accurate, understood inputs. Using analogRead() and reading pins means call analogread(a0) to get a 0–1023 integer. always validate by printing raw counts and converted voltage to the serial monitor before using values in control code.. In practical terms, how to capture raw adc counts from a0–a5 and validate readings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Converting ADC counts to a voltage is a straightforward calculation but critical to understand. The formula uses the raw integer from analogRead, divides by the top ADC index 1023.0 to produce a fraction of the reference, and multiplies by the reference voltage. With the default five volt reference the formula is float voltage = (analogRead(A0) / 1023.0) * 5.0. Use a floating point divisor so you keep fractional precision. A concrete example: if analogRead returns 143, divide 143 by 1023 giving about 0.1398, multiply by 5 to get about 0.699 volts. If you then have a sensor that produces 10 millivolts per degree, that voltage corresponds to roughly 69.9 degrees. Always pay attention to units: the formula produces volts, not millivolts or degrees. If you need millivolts multiply by 1000. If you need different reference voltage, replace 5.0 with your reference value. Finally, beware integer division: writing 1023 instead of 1023.0 can truncate results in some languages, so ensure floating arithmetic is used in the calculation. In practical terms, use the conversion formula and check units. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A potentiometer is one of the simplest analog sensors because it directly produces a voltage between two rails when you move the knob. It is a three‑pin device: one outer pin to 5V, the other outer pin to ground, and the middle pin gives a variable voltage that moves between 0 and 5 volts as you rotate the shaft. That movable terminal is the output the Arduino reads on an analog pin. Wiring it this way forms a voltage divider: a portion of the supply voltage appears at the center pin proportional to the knob position. This makes the potentiometer ideal for adjustable controls like volume, brightness, or speed. When wiring, ensure the middle pin goes to the analog input, and the ground and 5V rails are common with the Arduino. Also be mindful of mechanical limits: if the knob goes to an extreme and the ADC reports values near 0 or 1023, that is expected; if the values never reach extremes, check that the outer pins truly connect to 5V and ground. Finally, treat potentiometers as low-impedance sources for best readings and avoid long high-resistance wiring which can introduce noise.

Many sensors change resistance or output a small voltage in response to physical conditions. Light-dependent resistors and flex sensors typically change resistance and are read using a voltage divider. Temperature sensors like the LM35 or TMP36 produce a voltage that is proportional to temperature; the LM35 produces ten millivolts per degree Celsius as a simple example. The conversion pattern is consistent: read the ADC, convert counts to volts, then apply the sensor's scale factor to get the physical unit. For the LM35 example, a measured voltage of 0.699 V corresponds to about 69.9 degrees Celsius when using the ten millivolts per degree factor. Always check the sensor datasheet for the exact relationship and units because each sensor may have offsets or different scaling. When using resistive sensors like an LDR, select the fixed resistor in the divider so the voltage range matches the ADC steps you need. This lets your readings cover the useful range and improves sensitivity where you need it most. Other analog sensors and conversion means apply a two-step conversion: adc counts to volts, then volts to sensor units using the sensor's scale factor or datasheet formula.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Calibration makes sensor readings meaningful and comparable. A common two-point method for a light sensor is to record the ADC value in bright light and in complete darkness, then use those two measurements as your brightValue and darkValue. The map function rescales a raw ADC count from that measured range to a chosen target range such as 0 to 100 percent. For example, capture darkValue and brightValue, then write int percent = map(raw, darkValue, brightValue, 0, 100). Always ensure darkValue is less than brightValue. If you feed map reversed values the result will be inverted or unpredictable. Map performs integer scaling; if you need smooth fractional values, convert to float and compute scaling manually. Calibration also helps compensate for sensor variance and ambient conditions. For repeatable results, document your reference measurements, test at multiple points, and consider repeating calibration if environmental conditions change.
